newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries open lower as players book profits.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries open lower as players book profits.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries opened weaker on Wednesday as overseas players booked some profits after the market's four-day rally.
Still, traders noted Treasuries remained at the upper end of their recent ranges and that is unlikely to change for the next couple of sessions.
"How far can you take this (rally) with the (May) employment report coming out on Friday?" said Kevin Flanagan, money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
In early trade, the 30-year bond was at 96-23/32, down 6/32 from Tuesday, while its yield was up to 6.89 percent from 6.87.

In addition to profit-taking, Treasuries were lower due to some hedge fund selling, and hedging ahead of Ford Motor Co's upcoming 10-year bond offering. Weaker European bond markets were also weighing on Treasuries, players said.
But with little in the way of economic data this session, most agreed that there was a good shot the market's winning streak could reach five days.
"The consensus is that the good technical supply and demand factors will take the market higher," said a trader at a primary dealership.

The lone piece of data this session is April factory goods orders at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT, which traders deemed as a non-event. Economists look for a 0.8 percent increase after a 1.6 percent decrease in March.
Also of interest are a trio of Federal Reserve officials' speeches.

St. Louis Fed president is slated to speak at 1015 EDT in Arkansas, followed at 1300 EDT by a speech from Minneapolis Fed president Gary Stern, who will be in Milwaukee. At 1815 EDT, Richmond Fed president Al Broaddus will speak in Washington DC.

However, market participants said, reactions to the Fed officials' remarks should be muted. They noted that other remarks from Fed presidents in recent days -- such as from San Francisco's Robert Parry -- have been rather tame.
"There's plenty of room for interpretation," said one trader. "There seems to be something for everyone."

In early trading, bill rates were steady to one basis point lower. The two-year note was at 100-3/32, down 1/32, to yield 6.20 percent. The five-year note was down 2/32 to 100-2/32 to yield 6.49 percent and the 10-year note was at 99-30/32, down 4/32, to yield 6.63 percent.
